what: Part 1. Is there a SIDS cluster in North Carolina?
title: Cluster detection and surveillance
text: data. Sudden infant death syndrome deaths live births 100 North Carolina counties, 1974-78 1979-84 (nc_sids). question: deaths concentrated anywhere births predict? epi_spatial_scan() places circles several radii around every county centroid, finds circle largest Poisson likelihood ratio, compares largest ratio datasets simulated clustering. scan runs compiled C++, 999 simulations take well second.  periods show significant cluster south-east state: 1974-78 covers Robeson, Bladen Columbus counties, 1979-84 neighboring Scotland County. Excess SIDS mortality part North Carolina long-noted feature dataset.
code: set.seed(2024) scan74 <- epi_spatial_scan(nc_sids, x_km, y_km, sids_1974, births_1974,                            radii = c(30, 60, 90), nsim = 999) scan79 <- epi_spatial_scan(nc_sids, x_km, y_km, sids_1979, births_1979,                            radii = c(30, 60, 90), nsim = 999) knitr::kable(   rbind(cbind(period = "1974-78", scan74), cbind(period = "1979-84", scan79))[     c("period", "center_x", "center_y", "radius", "observed", "expected", "relative_risk", "p_value")],   digits = 2 ) draw_circle <- function(s, label) {   t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)   data.frame(x = s$center_x + s$radius * cos(t), y = s$center_y + s$radius * sin(t), period = label) } circles <- rbind(draw_circle(scan74, "1974-78"), draw_circle(scan79, "1979-84")) nc_sids$rate <- 1000 * nc_sids$sids_1974 / nc_sids$births_1974 ggplot(nc_sids, aes(x_km, y_km)) +   geom_point(aes(size = births_1974, colour = rate), alpha = 0.85) +   geom_path(data = circles, aes(x, y, linetype = period), colour = red, linewidth = 1) +   scale_colour_gradient(low = "#F4D9D6", high = red, name = "SIDS per 1,000\nbirths, 1974-78") +   scale_size_area(max_size = 9, guide = "none") +   coord_equal() +   labs(x = "Easting (km)", y = "Northing (km)", linetype = "Most likely cluster") +   theme_minimal()

what: Part 2. Where and when did COVID-19 cluster in New York State?
title: Cluster detection and surveillance
text: data. Weekly confirmed COVID-19 cases New York’s 62 counties 13 weeks spring 2020, county populations (ny_covid_counties_2020). question: area run recent weeks greatest excess? epi_spacetime_scan() adds time window: considers every circle together every window recent weeks.  cluster five boroughs New York City plus Nassau County first ten weeks, epicenter United States’ spring 2020 wave.
code: set.seed(2020) st <- epi_spacetime_scan(ny_covid_counties_2020, x_km, y_km, week_0308:week_0531, population,                          radii = c(20, 50, 100), nsim = 199) knitr::kable(st[c("radius", "window", "observed", "expected", "relative_risk", "p_value")], digits = 3) ny <- ny_covid_counties_2020 inside <- sqrt((ny$x_km - st$center_x)^2 + (ny$y_km - st$center_y)^2) <= st$radius ny$in_cluster <- ifelse(inside, "Cluster", "Outside") ny$rate <- 1e5 * rowSums(ny[grep("^week_", names(ny))]) / ny$population ggplot(ny, aes(x_km, y_km)) +   geom_point(aes(size = population, colour = rate, shape = in_cluster), alpha = 0.9) +   scale_colour_gradient(low = "#DCE4EE", high = red, name = "Cases per\n100,000") +   scale_size_area(max_size = 10, guide = "none") +   scale_shape_manual(values = c(Cluster = 17, Outside = 16), name = NULL) +   coord_equal() +   labs(x = "Easting (km)", y = "Northing (km)", title = "Cumulative COVID-19 incidence, 8 March to 31 May 2020") +   theme_minimal()

what: Part 3. Screening monthly deaths against a seasonal baseline
title: Cluster detection and surveillance
text: data. Monthly deaths bronchitis, emphysema asthma UK, 1974-79 (datasets::ldeaths). question: months 1978-79 unusually high, given strong winter seasonality? Fit seasonal baseline 1974-77 , screen 1978-79. negative binomial baseline allows overdispersion, Holm’s adjustment controls chance false alert 24 months screened.  month 1978-79 exceeds seasonal pattern predicts.
code: uk <- data.frame(time = as.numeric(time(datasets::ldeaths)), deaths = as.numeric(datasets::ldeaths)) training <- subset(uk, time < 1978) screen <- subset(uk, time >= 1978) s <- epi_seasonal_surveillance(screen, time, deaths, training = training, period = 1,                                harmonics = 2, family = "negbin", adjust = "holm") sum(s$alert) #> [1] 0  ggplot(uk, aes(time, deaths)) +   geom_line(colour = navy) +   geom_line(data = s, aes(y = threshold), colour = red, linetype = 2) +   geom_line(data = s, aes(y = baseline_expected), colour = red) +   geom_vline(xintercept = 1978, linetype = 3) +   labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per month",        subtitle = "Observed (blue), seasonal baseline and alert threshold fitted on 1974-77 (red)") +   theme_minimal()

what: 1. Smoking and coronary deaths: rates and confounding
title: Cohort and clinical epidemiology
text: study. Male British doctors followed ten years, coronary deaths person-years age smoking (british_doctors; Doll Hill). question: much higher coronary mortality among smokers?  crude rate ratio (1.72) overstates effect smokers cohort older average; adjusting age gives 1.43 (95% CI 1.15 1.76). age-specific ratios show effect modification (interaction p = 0.04): smoking multiplies coronary mortality almost sixfold 35-44, twofold 45-54, little relative effect 75-84, baseline risk high everyone.
code: bd <- british_doctors bd$rate <- 1000 * bd$deaths / bd$person_years ggplot(bd, aes(age_group, rate, colour = factor(smoker, labels = c("Non-smoker", "Smoker")), group = smoker)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c(navy, red), name = NULL) +   scale_y_log10() +   labs(x = "Age group", y = "Deaths per 1,000 person-years (log scale)") +   theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top") models <- dplyr::bind_rows(   epi_adjusted_rate_ratio(bd, deaths, person_years, smoker),   epi_adjusted_rate_ratio(bd, deaths, person_years, smoker, adjust = age_group),   epi_adjusted_rate_ratio(bd, deaths, person_years, smoker, adjust = age_group, modifier = age_group) ) knitr::kable(models[c("modifier_level", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high", "interaction_p_value")],              digits = 3)

title: Cohort and clinical epidemiology
text: study. 1,384 patients monoclonal gammopathy undetermined significance Mayo Clinic (survival::mgus2). Patients can progress plasma-cell malignancy die first.  Censoring deaths overstates risk progression, patients die can longer progress: 20 years naive estimate 21%, twice correct cumulative incidence 10%. cumulative incidence function answers question patients actually ask.
code: m <- survival::mgus2 m$years <- ifelse(m$pstat == 0, m$futime, m$ptime) / 12 m$event <- ifelse(m$pstat == 0, 2 * m$death, 1) m$ev_any <- as.integer(m$event == 1)  aj <- epi_cumulative_incidence(m, years, event, cause = 1) km <- epi_kaplan_meier(m, years, ev_any) compare <- rbind(   data.frame(years = aj$time, risk = aj$cumulative_incidence, method = "Aalen-Johansen (correct)"),   data.frame(years = km$time, risk = 1 - km$estimate, method = "1 - Kaplan-Meier (deaths censored)") ) ggplot(compare, aes(years, risk, colour = method)) +   geom_step(linewidth = 1) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c(red, navy), name = NULL) +   labs(x = "Years since diagnosis", y = "Cumulative risk of progression") +   theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Cohort and clinical epidemiology
text: Fit logistic model Pima training data evaluate independent test set (MASS::Pima.tr, MASS::Pima.te).   model well calibrated (calibration slope 0.95, AUC 0.86) offers net benefit treating everyone one every threshold shown.
code: train <- MASS::Pima.tr test <- MASS::Pima.te train$dm <- as.integer(train$type == "Yes") test$dm <- as.integer(test$type == "Yes") fit <- glm(dm ~ glu + bmi + age + ped, binomial, train) test$risk <- predict(fit, test, type = "response")  epi_calibration_summary(test, dm, risk) #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #>       n event_prevalence brier calibration_in_large calibration_intercept #>   <int>            <dbl> <dbl>                <dbl>                 <dbl> #> 1   332            0.328 0.142              -0.0599               -0.0855 #> # ℹ 2 more variables: calibration_slope <dbl>, roc_auc <dbl> cal <- epi_calibration(test, dm, risk, bins = 5) ggplot(cal, aes(mean_predicted, observed_risk)) +   geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +   geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf_low, ymax = conf_high), colour = red) +   coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +   labs(x = "Predicted risk", y = "Observed risk (95% CI)", title = "Calibration on the test set") +   theme_minimal() dc <- epi_decision_curve(test, dm, risk, thresholds = seq(0.05, 0.6, 0.01)) ggplot(dc, aes(threshold, net_benefit, colour = strategy)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) +   coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.05, 0.35)) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c(model = red, treat_all = navy, treat_none = "grey50"), name = NULL) +   labs(x = "Risk threshold for action", y = "Net benefit", title = "Decision curve") +   theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")

title: COVID-19 outbreak analysis
text: renewal equation needs generation-interval distribution. gamma distribution mean 5 days, discretized two weeks: Early cases mostly travelers infected abroad. Treat case case previous 14 days imported, seeds transmission without counted local transmission:  Rt well 1 lockdown fell 1 within two weeks .
code: w <- dgamma(1:14, shape = 2.3, rate = 0.45) w <- w / sum(w) nz <- nz_covid_2020 recent <- stats::filter(c(rep(0, 14), nz$cases), rep(1, 14), sides = 1) nz$imported <- ifelse(recent[14 + seq_len(nrow(nz)) - 1] == 0, nz$cases, 0L) nz$local <- nz$cases - nz$imported  rt <- epi_rt_gamma(nz, local, weights = w, window = 7, imported = imported) subset(rt, date %in% as.Date(c("2020-03-25", "2020-04-08", "2020-04-22")),        c(date, rt_mean, rt_low, rt_high)) #> # A tibble: 3 × 4 #>   date       rt_mean rt_low rt_high #>   <date>       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> #> 1 2020-03-25   3.34   2.88    3.84  #> 2 2020-04-08   1.01   0.928   1.11  #> 3 2020-04-22   0.439  0.340   0.552 ggplot(subset(rt, !is.na(rt_mean) & date <= as.Date("2020-05-15")), aes(date, rt_mean)) +   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rt_low, ymax = rt_high), fill = red, alpha = 0.2) +   geom_line(colour = red, linewidth = 1) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +   geom_vline(xintercept = lockdown, linetype = 2, colour = navy) +   labs(x = NULL, y = expression(R[t] ~ "(95% credible interval)")) +   theme_minimal()

title: Get started with tidyepidemio
text: tep_advise() says estimator answers question check first; tep_interpret() explains result, says next report paper. tidyvisor package installed, tidyvisor() calls .
code: d <- data.frame(exposure = rep(0:1, each = 40),                 outcome = rep(c(0, 1, 0, 1), c(30, 10, 18, 22))) tep_advise(d, exposure = "exposure", outcome = "outcome") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: is the exposure associated with the outcome? ───────────────────── #> Question: association #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Records: 80 #> • Outcome events: 32 of 80 (40.0%) — common outcome (over 10%): odds ratios #>   exaggerate risk ratios; report the risk ratio #> • Exposure groups: 0: 40, 1: 40 #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Estimate: Risk ratio (cohort) or odds ratio (case-control) #> The design decides the measure: risks in cohorts and trials, odds in #> case-control studies; rates when follow-up time differs. #> epi_risk_ratio(data, exposure, outcome)   # or epi_odds_ratio(), epi_rate_ratio() #> Confounding: Stratify or adjust #> A crude ratio mixes the exposure with whatever travels with it; compare it with #> the Mantel-Haenszel or adjusted ratio. #> epi_mantel_haenszel(data, exposure, outcome, <stratum>) #> Small numbers: Exact test when cells are small #> With expected counts below 5, use an exact test and interval. #> epi_fisher_test(data, exposure, outcome) tep_interpret(epi_risk_ratio(d, exposure, outcome)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • The risk ratio is 2.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 4.03). The risk of the outcome is 120% #>   higher in the exposed than in the unexposed. #> • A crude estimate: confounding is not removed. #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • Check that the association is not explained by confounding: stratify #>   (epi_mantel_haenszel()) or adjust (epi_adjusted_risk_ratio(), #>   epi_adjusted_odds_ratio()) for the confounders named in advance, and report #>   crude and adjusted estimates side by side. #> • With several exposure levels, report each against the same reference group, #>   and test for a trend if the levels are ordered, rather than testing every #>   pair. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results: 'The risk ratio for exposure was 2.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 4.03).' #> • Report the estimate with its 95% CI (and the counts behind it), not the #>   p-value alone; give crude and adjusted estimates side by side. #> • Figure: a forest plot of the estimates with their intervals on a log scale, #>   with a line at 1: #> • ggplot2::autoplot(result) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: one column (about 85 mm) or the page (about 180 #>   mm); axes labelled with units; a color-blind-safe palette; intervals shown, #>   with what they are stated in the caption; text at least 8 pt; vector PDF. #> • Table: exposed and unexposed with events and totals (or person-time), the #>   crude and adjusted estimates with intervals, and what was adjusted for. #> • Methods: the design (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), the measure and #>   why, the interval method, the confounders and how they were chosen; follow #>   STROBE for observational studies, and the software (R 4.6.2, tidyepidemio #>   1.2.0.9000; citation("tidyepidemio")).

text: Descriptive, analytic infectious-disease epidemiology one tidy workflow: data frames , tibbles . Documentation: https://tidyepidemio.in4metrix.dev/ Epidemiology R spread across many packages, input format output object: epitools Epi 2x2 tables, survival cmprsk time--event data, EpiEstim Rt, surveillance outbreak detection, SaTScan (outside R) cluster detection. tidyepidemio puts core methods behind one consistent interface. Every function takes data frame unquoted column names returns tibble, results go straight dplyr, ggplot2 reports. slow inner loops run compiled C++, results checked established reference implementations (see Validation). Measures association: risk, odds rate ratios, Mantel-Haenszel Breslow-Day, adjusted logistic, modified-Poisson Poisson models weights, robust cluster errors, effect modification splines. Survival competing risks: Kaplan-Meier, cumulative incidence delayed entry Aalen-Johansen intervals, Cox models, RMST. Clinical epidemiology: diagnostic accuracy, ROC AUC, calibration, decision curves. Infectious disease dynamics: epidemic curves, growth rate, Rt, SIR/SEIR fitting simulation, nowcasting forecasting. Surveillance clusters: seasonal moving-window screens, CUSUM, Kulldorff-type spatial space-time scan statistics.
